title: A Headline Number Is a Summary
paragraphs: The claim that many living people carry Neanderthal DNA has become so familiar that its limits are easily forgotten. The full picture is more careful and more interesting. Early estimates, reported after the first Neanderthal genome was sequenced in twenty ten, suggested that between one and four percent of the ancestry of non-Africans came from Neanderthals. A later analysis, published in the journal Cell in twenty twenty, refined the figures: roughly one point seven to one point eight percent of European and Asian genomes.

The same study overturned a second assumption. Africans in the sample, long thought to carry almost no Neanderthal DNA, were found to carry an average of about seventeen million Neanderthal base pairs, roughly a third of the amount found in Europeans and Asians. The authors argued that gene flow had run in both directions, so some of the Neanderthal-like sequences in Africa may have travelled back with early modern humans. Gene flow in both directions complicates any simple story about who gave what to whom.

Responsible readers should note the caveats. The team sampled only a limited number of African populations, so the results may not apply to everyone with African ancestry. Moreover, the Neanderthal genome used for comparison came from Siberia, which may not have been part of the population that actually mixed with migrating humans. Such qualifications do not undermine the central finding; they simply remind us that a headline number is a summary, not a verdict. A careful reader will therefore treat each percentage as an estimate that may be revised.
